task1.title: Reasons for UK university study
task1.prompt: The charts below show the reasons of students to study a particular in a UK university in the year 1987 and 2007.

chartDesc.title: Reasons why students chose a college or university, UK
chartDesc.overview: Suitable degree courses was the main reason for choosing a college or university in both 1987 and 2007. Over the 20-year period, being close to parental home grew significantly in importance, while good sports and social activities saw a sharp decline.
keyFeatures: In 1987, 'Suitable degree courses' was the top reason at 35%, followed by 'Quality of resources' (21%) and 'Good sports and social activities' (19%).
In 2007, 'Suitable degree courses' remained the highest category at 37%, while 'Good sports and social activities' fell dramatically to just 6%.
'Close to parental home' more than doubled from 10% in 1987 to 22% in 2007, becoming the second most common reason.
'Quality teaching' rose slightly from 15% in 1987 to 18% in 2007, whereas 'Quality of resources' decreased from 21% to 17%.

task1.instruction: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparison where relevant.
task1.sampleBand5:
The charts show the reasons students studied in UK universities in 1987 and 2007. It is clear that some reasons are more popular than others.

In 1987, the main reason was job opportunities, at 40%. The second reason was further study at 20%. Career promotion was also a reason, but it was much less at only 15%. Other reasons are specified as other which was 25%.

In 2007, job opportunities was still the main reason, but it increased to 50%. Further study was still a reason, but not as much as before, it decreased to 15%. Career promotion was the same, at 15%. The other reasons was decreased to 20%. So, the main change is that job opportunities became more important and further study became less important. The other reasons changed.
task1.sampleBand6:
The pie charts give information about the reasons why students chose to study at UK universities in 1987 and 2007. The data is divided into several categories such as to get a better job, interested in subject or for career prospects.

Overall, it is clear that the main reason for studying was to get a better job in both years. However, there were some changes in the importance of other reasons. In 1987, 34% of students said they studied to get a better job, which was the biggest reason. In contrast, the percentage increased to 40% in 2007. Career prospects was the second most important reason in 1987, at just over 20%, but this dropped to around 15% in 2007.

Interest in the subject was a significant factor, with around 18% in 1987 and a similar percentage in 2007. While influence of friends and family was a smaller percentage in both years, it saw a slight decline from 10% to 7%. Other reasons accounted for a relatively small proportion, with around 16% in 1987 and 19% in 2007. The data shows that economic reasons became more important over the 20-year period.
task1.sampleBand7:
The pie charts illustrate the primary reasons why students chose to study at UK universities in 1987 and 2007. Overall, while 'to get a better job' was the most significant factor in both years, its dominance increased considerably over the two decades. Conversely, the importance of other factors diminished.

In 1987, the most prevalent reason for studying in the UK was to secure better employment opportunities, accounting for 40% of the responses. This was followed by a general interest in the subject, which motivated 23% of students. Academic reputation and career advancement were equally influential, each attracting 15% of students. Finally, a mere 7% cited other reasons.

By 2007, the proportion of students motivated by future job prospects had risen sharply to 60%. Interest in the subject saw a corresponding decrease, falling to 15%. The percentage of students influenced by academic reputation and career prospects both experienced a decline to 8%. The remaining 'other' reasons made up 9% of the total. It is evident that the focus on career outcomes intensified over this period, overshadowing other motivations for pursuing higher education.

The pie charts illustrate the primary motivations for students choosing to study at UK universities in 1987 and 2007. Overall, career prospects and interest in the subject were the dominant factors in both years; however, the relative importance of each shifted noticeably over the two decades.

In 1987, the predominant reason for university study was future job opportunities, accounting for 45% of responses. Interest in the subject was also significant, representing 30%. The influence of better career prospects increased considerably over time, rising to 53% in 2007. Conversely, the proportion of students driven by subject interest declined, although it remained a substantial factor at 22%.

Other reasons played a comparatively minor role. Advice from family and friends motivated 12% of students in 1987, decreasing to 9% in 2007. Similarly, both the percentage of students influenced by teachers and those seeking a better understanding of the subject experienced a decline, from 8% to 6% and from 5% to 4%, respectively. It is noteworthy that, despite these fluctuations, career aspirations consistently held the most sway over students' decisions, underscoring the perceived link between higher education and employment. The charts also suggest a marginal increase in the focus on career paths as the primary motivation for university education.

The charts illustrate the primary motivations behind students choosing to study specific subjects at a UK university in 1987 and 2007. Overall, career prospects consistently ranked as the leading factor, although its dominance diminished over the two decades, while interest in the subject matter and recommendations from others gained prominence.

In 1987, by far the most significant reason was 'better career prospects', cited by 52% of students. 'Interest in the subject' was the next most popular reason, accounting for 22% of responses. Recommendations from school or family held a relatively minor influence, at 11%, while a mere 7% were motivated by the belief that the subject was 'easy'. The remaining 8% indicated 'other' reasons.

By 2007, the landscape had shifted somewhat. While 'better career prospects' remained the top reason, its proportion had decreased to 34%. 'Interest in the subject' saw a notable increase, rising to 30%, indicating a growing emphasis on personal fulfillment. Recommendations also experienced a substantial surge, reaching 16%. The perceived ease of the subject held steady at 7%, and 'other' reasons accounted for the remaining 13%. It is evident that the weight given to career advancement decreased, while intrinsic interest and external advice became increasingly influential drivers in subject selection.
task1.sampleAnswer:
The bar charts compare the primary motivations for students enrolling at a specific UK university in 1987 and 2007. Overall, it is evident that while interest in the subject remained the dominant factor in both years, there was a significant shift toward employment-related motivations by 2007. Conversely, more personal or social reasons for studying saw a decline in popularity over the twenty-year period.

In 1987, 'Interest in the subject' was the single most cited reason, with nearly 45% of students choosing this option. By 2007, this figure dropped slightly to approximately 40%, yet it remained the most prevalent motivation. In contrast, 'Career prospects' saw a substantial increase, rising from just under 20% in 1987 to nearly 35% in 2007, highlighting a growing focus on the professional utility of higher education.

Other motivations such as 'Parental pressure' and 'Social life' experienced a downward trend. Parental influence fell from 15% to a mere 5%, while the desire for a social life as a primary driver decreased from 10% to around 7%. Interestingly, 'Lack of other options' emerged as a more significant factor in 2007, doubling from 5% to 10%. This suggests that for a tenth of the student body, university had become a default choice rather than a proactive pursuit.

task2.title: Unemployment vs unsatisfying jobs
task2.prompt: It is better for people to be unemployed than people to be employed but they do not enjoy. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
task2.instruction: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
task2.sampleBand5:
Some people think it is good if people are not working and some people think it is good if people are working even if they don't like it. I think it is better to work even if you don't like it.

If you are not working, you don't get money. This is a problem because you need money to buy food and pay for your house. If you don't have a job, it is very hard to live. You might have to ask your family for money, and this can make them sad or angry. Also, if you don't work, you might feel sad because you are not doing anything useful.

When you work, even if you don't like the job, you can still get money. This money can help you to live and buy things you need. Also, working can help you to meet new people and learn new things. Even if the job is boring, you can still learn something. For example, you can learn how to work with other people or how to use a computer. These skills can help you to get a better job in the future.

Some people say that if you don't like your job, you will be very sad and stressed. This is true, but it is still better than not having a job at all. You can always look for a new job while you are working. It is important to try to find a job that you like, but it is better to have a job that you don't like than to have no job at all. So, I think people should try to work even if they don’t enjoy it.
task2.sampleBand6:
The question of whether it is preferable to be unemployed or employed in an unfulfilling job is a complex one. While employment provides financial stability and a sense of purpose, being stuck in a job that one dislikes can have negative impacts on mental and physical health. I believe that while unemployment presents challenges, it can be a better option than being employed in a job that brings no satisfaction.

On the one hand, having a job, even if it is not ideal, provides a regular income which is essential for survival in today's world. It allows individuals to meet their basic needs such as food, shelter, and clothing. Furthermore, employment can offer social interaction and a sense of belonging. Many people find that their colleagues become their friends, and the workplace provides a sense of community. However, these benefits can be overshadowed by the negative effects of being in a job that one hates.

On the other hand, being unemployed, while initially stressful, can provide an opportunity for self-reflection and exploration. Individuals can use this time to identify their passions and interests, and to develop new skills. They might, for example, take online courses, volunteer for a cause they believe in, or start their own business. This period of unemployment can be seen as an investment in their future, leading to a more fulfilling career in the long run. The strain of a job you hate can also cause high stress levels.

Of course, unemployment also has its downsides. The lack of income can lead to financial hardship and social isolation. However, with the right support system and a proactive approach, these challenges can be overcome. Ultimately, I think that the freedom to pursue one's passions and the avoidance of a soul-crushing job outweigh the financial security that an unfulfilling job provides. It is probably better to be unemployed.
task2.sampleBand7:
The question of whether unemployment is preferable to unhappy employment is a complex one. While the ideal situation is undoubtedly fulfilling work, I believe that, in some circumstances, being unemployed can be a better option, although this is not universally true. I agree with this statement to a considerable extent, primarily because of the detrimental effects of job dissatisfaction on mental health and the potential for unemployed individuals to pursue more fulfilling avenues.

Firstly, prolonged unhappiness in a job can have a significant negative impact on an individual's mental well-being. Constant stress, lack of job satisfaction, and feelings of being undervalued can lead to anxiety, depression, and burnout. In such cases, the financial security offered by employment may be outweighed by the damage to one's psychological health. An individual who is unemployed, while facing financial challenges, has the opportunity to focus on self-care, pursue personal interests, and seek out more suitable employment options. This period of unemployment can be a chance for reflection and re-evaluation, leading to a more positive and fulfilling future.

However, it is important to acknowledge the significant downsides of unemployment. The financial strain and social stigma associated with being out of work can also be detrimental to mental health. Furthermore, long-term unemployment can erode skills and confidence, making it harder to re-enter the workforce. Therefore, the decision to leave an unsatisfying job should not be taken lightly and should be carefully considered in light of one's financial situation and alternative employment prospects. It’s also worth noting that some people find satisfaction in aspects of their lives outside of work, which can mitigate the negative effects of a job they dislike.

In conclusion, while employment provides financial stability and a sense of purpose for many, I maintain that being unemployed is sometimes a more viable option than remaining in a job that causes significant distress. The potential for improved mental health and the opportunity to pursue more fulfilling paths can outweigh the financial disadvantages, provided that the period of unemployment is used productively and with a clear plan for the future. Ultimately, the optimal choice depends on individual circumstances and priorities.
task2.sampleBand8:
The debate regarding the relative merits of unemployment versus unsatisfying employment is a complex one, with valid arguments on both sides. While the financial security and social interaction that employment provides are undoubtedly beneficial, I tend to believe that being unemployed is preferable to being trapped in a job that one actively dislikes. This is primarily because of the detrimental effects of unfulfilling work on mental and physical well-being, and the potential for unemployed individuals to pursue more meaningful opportunities.

Firstly, being employed in a job that one finds deeply unsatisfying can have profoundly negative consequences for an individual's mental health. The constant stress and lack of fulfillment can lead to burnout, anxiety, and even depression. Furthermore, the negative emotions associated with a disliked job can spill over into other aspects of life, affecting relationships and overall happiness. For example, a study by the University of Warwick found a strong correlation between job dissatisfaction and increased risk of mental health problems. In contrast, while unemployment can certainly be stressful, it also offers the opportunity for self-reflection and the pursuit of activities that bring joy and purpose.

Secondly, unemployment, while challenging, can be a catalyst for positive change. It provides individuals with the time and space to reassess their skills, interests, and career goals. They can use this period to upskill or reskill, explore new career paths, or even start their own businesses. Indeed, many successful entrepreneurs have attributed their success to being forced to reconsider their options after losing a job. This period of unemployment allows for self-directed learning and the exploration of opportunities that might never have been considered while stuck in a dead-end job. The freedom to learn and grow can be incredibly empowering.

Admittedly, the financial hardships associated with unemployment cannot be ignored. However, government support programs and personal savings can provide a safety net while individuals seek more suitable employment. Moreover, the long-term benefits of finding a fulfilling career, in terms of both personal happiness and professional success, outweigh the short-term financial challenges of unemployment. It’s also worth noting that many people in unfulfilling jobs experience a form of ‘presenteeism,’ where they are physically present but mentally disengaged, costing companies productivity and potentially hindering their own career progression. This ultimately suggests that a proactive approach to finding meaningful work, even if it involves a period of unemployment, is a more sustainable and beneficial strategy.

In conclusion, while the security of employment is valuable, I firmly believe that being unemployed is preferable to being stuck in a job that one hates. The detrimental effects on mental and physical health, coupled with the opportunity for self-discovery and career reinvention, make unemployment a potentially positive, albeit challenging, experience. Ultimately, prioritizing personal well-being and long-term fulfillment is more important than simply holding onto a job that provides only dissatisfaction.
task2.sampleBand9:
The assertion that unemployment is preferable to employment devoid of enjoyment presents a complex dichotomy. While the detrimental effects of unfulfilling work on mental and physical well-being cannot be understated, the financial and psychological burdens of unemployment also warrant careful consideration. I believe that while job satisfaction is undeniably crucial, the complete dismissal of employment in its absence is an oversimplification, and a more nuanced approach is required.

On the one hand, the corrosive impact of a job that offers no personal fulfillment can be profound. Individuals trapped in such situations often experience chronic stress, leading to burnout, depression, and a diminished sense of self-worth. Furthermore, a lack of engagement can stifle creativity and innovation, ultimately hindering professional growth. In extreme cases, this can even manifest in physical ailments stemming from prolonged exposure to a toxic or demoralizing work environment. Therefore, the argument that unemployment, despite its challenges, might be a healthier alternative in such circumstances holds a degree of validity.

However, the reality of unemployment is often far from idyllic. The lack of financial security can lead to significant stress, impacting not only the individual but also their family. Furthermore, prolonged unemployment can erode self-esteem and lead to social isolation, creating a vicious cycle of negativity. The absence of a structured routine and the sense of purpose that employment provides can also be detrimental to mental health. Moreover, the increasingly competitive job market means that extended periods of unemployment can significantly damage future career prospects. Therefore, to suggest that this situation is universally preferable to even an unfulfilling job is a gross overstatement.

Ultimately, the optimal solution lies not in choosing between these two extremes, but in striving to find employment that aligns with one's values and interests. This may involve proactive career planning, seeking opportunities for professional development, or even considering a career change. While the ideal of universally fulfilling employment may remain elusive, individuals can take steps to mitigate the negative effects of unfulfilling work by focusing on personal growth, seeking support from colleagues and mentors, and cultivating a healthy work-life balance. A pragmatic approach necessitates recognizing the inherent challenges of both scenarios and actively pursuing solutions that prioritize both financial stability and personal well-being. To summarily dismiss employment, regardless of its perceived lack of fulfillment, is to ignore the significant benefits it provides and the potential for positive change within the workplace. The key lies in actively seeking avenues for improvement and personal growth within one's chosen profession or exploring alternative career paths that offer greater satisfaction. This constitutes a far more constructive approach than simply opting out of the workforce altogether.
task2.sampleAnswer:
The question of whether an unsatisfactory job is preferable to having no job at all is a complex one, touching upon economic necessity and psychological well-being. While I acknowledge that chronic job dissatisfaction can lead to severe mental health issues, I largely disagree with the notion that unemployment is a better alternative, primarily due to the financial and social repercussions of being without work.

On the one hand, proponents of the idea that unemployment is better often point to the corrosive effects of a toxic work environment. Spending forty hours a week in a role that one loathes can lead to burnout, depression, and a diminished sense of self-worth. In such cases, the stress of the job may outweigh the salary earned, potentially damaging one's health and personal relationships. From a purely psychological standpoint, being free from a debilitating work environment allows an individual the mental space to recover and seek a more fulfilling career path.

However, the reality of unemployment is often far more grueling than a disliked job. Financial stability is the cornerstone of a functional life; without a steady income, individuals face the immediate stress of being unable to meet basic needs like housing and nutrition. Furthermore, a long-term gap in a CV can make future employment significantly harder to secure, creating a cycle of poverty and exclusion. Employment, even if unrewarding, provides a structured routine and a sense of social participation that is often lost when one is out of work. In most societies, a job also provides access to vital benefits such as healthcare and pension contributions.

In conclusion, while I agree that no one should remain in a miserable job indefinitely, I believe that being employed in an unenjoyable role is generally a more sustainable position than being unemployed. The practical and financial advantages of work typically provide a more secure foundation for eventually transitioning to a more satisfying career than the precarious state of unemployment ever could.

Ba'zi odamlar odamlar ishlamasa yaxshi deb hisoblaydi va ba'zi odamlar o'ylaydi odamlar ishlasa yaxshi, hatto ularga yoqmasa ham. Menimcha, hatto yoqmasa ham ishlash yaxshiroq.

Agar siz ishlamasangiz, siz pul topmaysiz. Bu muammo, chunki sizga oziq-ovqat sotib olish va uyingiz uchun to'lash uchun pul kerak. Agar sizda ishingiz bo'lmasa, yashash juda qiyin. Bundan tashqari, agar siz ishlamasangiz, foydali ish qilmayotganingiz uchun xafa bo'lishingiz mumkin.

Qachonki siz ishlasangiz, hatto bu ish sizga yoqmasa ham, siz hali ham pul topishingiz mumkin. Bu pul sizga yashashga va kerakli narsalarni sotib olishga yordam beradi. Shuningdek, ishlash yangi odamlar bilan tanishishga va yangi narsalarni o'rganishga yordam beradi. Ish zerikarli bo'lsa ham, siz hali ham nimadir o'rganishingiz mumkin. Misol uchun, siz boshqa odamlar bilan qanday ishlashni yoki kompyuterdan qanday foydalanishni o'rganishingiz mumkin. Bu ko'nikmalar sizga kelajakda yaxshiroq ish topishga yordam beradi.

Ba'zi odamlar agar ishingiz sizga yoqmasa, juda xafa va stressda bo'lasiz deyishadi. Bu to'g'ri, lekin bu umuman ishsiz bo'lishdan ko'ra yaxshiroq. Ishlayotganingizda har doim yangi ish qidirishingiz mumkin. Muhim o'zingizga yoqadigan ish topishga harakat qilish, lekin umuman ishsiz bo'lishdan ko'ra yoqmaydigan ishingiz bo'lgani yaxshiroq.
